<!-- Section 2: Theory -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-theory">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">01 · Nonlinear Dynamics</div>
<h2>5.1 The Exact Simple Pendulum</h2>
<p>For a point mass $m$ suspended by a rigid, massless rod of length $L$ swinging in a vertical plane under gravity $g$:</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<div class="eq-box">
$$\ddot{\theta}(t) + \omega_0^2 \sin\theta(t) = 0, \quad \omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}$$
</div>

<p>
Multiplying by $\dot{\theta}$ and integrating once with respect to time yields the Hamiltonian energy conservation law:
</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$E = \frac{1}{2} m L^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + m g L (1 - \cos\theta) = \text{constant}$$
</div>

<p>
Unlike the harmonic oscillator where period $T_0 = 2\pi/\omega_0$ is completely independent of amplitude (isochronous), the nonlinear pendulum's period stretches as initial release angle $\theta_0$ increases:
</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$T(\theta_0) = \frac{4}{\omega_0} K\left(\sin\frac{\theta_0}{2}\right) = T_0 \left(1 + \frac{1}{16}\theta_0^2 + \frac{11}{3072}\theta_0^4 + \dots\right)$$
</div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 3: Phase Space -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-phase">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">02 · Geometric Topology</div>
<h2>5.2 Cylindrical Phase Space & The Homoclinic Separatrix</h2>
<p>The state plane $(\theta, \dot{\theta})$ is naturally $2\pi$-periodic in angle, forming a phase cylinder.</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<div class="callout">
<strong>• Closed Libration Orbits ($E < 2mgL$):</strong> Concentric oval orbits around the stable downward center $(0,0)$ representing bounded back-and-forth oscillation.<br>
<strong>• The Homoclinic Separatrix ($E = 2mgL$):</strong> Critical energy boundary connecting the unstable inverted upright equilibrium points $(\pm\pi, 0)$. A trajectory released exactly on the separatrix requires infinite time ($T \to \infty$) to reach the apex.<br>
<strong>• Continuous Whirling Motion ($E > 2mgL$):</strong> Open, undulating phase trajectories where the pendulum has sufficient kinetic energy to spin over the top continuously.
</div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 4: Misconceptions -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-misconceptions">
<div class="callout-important">
<div class="callout-title">
<svg width="20" height="20" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><path d="M10.29 3.86L1.82 18a2 2 0 0 0 1.71 3h16.94a2 2 0 0 0 1.71-3L13.71 3.86a2 2 0 0 0-3.42 0z"/><line x1="12" y1="9" x2="12" y2="13"/><line x1="12" y1="17" x2="12.01" y2="17"/></svg>
Common Misconception · Is the Small-Angle Approximation Valid up to 45°?
</div>
<p style="margin: 0 0 8px 0;">
Textbooks often claim $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ is acceptable for "small angles," leading engineers to apply it casually up to $45^\circ$.
</p>
<p style="margin: 0;">
At $\theta_0 = 45^\circ$ ($0.785\text{ rad}$), the period error is already $+3.9\%$. In precision clockwork or seismic sensors, this accumulates into massive phase drift over several cycles! For $\theta_0 = 90^\circ$, the exact period is $+18.0\%$ longer than $T_0$, and at $\theta_0 = 175^\circ$, the period is more than $300\%$ longer!
</p>
</div>
</section>

<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-quiz">

<h2>5.3 Check Your Understanding</h2>
<p>Test your understanding of nonlinear pendulum dynamics.</p>
</div>

<div class="quiz-box">
<div class="quiz-question">
<strong>Question:</strong> What happens to the period $T(\theta_0)$ of a conservative simple pendulum as the initial release angle $\theta_0 \to \pi$ ($180^\circ$ upright)?
</div>
<div class="quiz-options">
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="false" data-explanation="Period elongation is dramatic and unbounded near the inverted equilibrium point!">
A. It remains equal to the linear period $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$.
</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="true" data-explanation="As theta0 approaches pi, the trajectory approaches the homoclinic separatrix orbit entering the saddle point (pi, 0). Near a saddle fixed point, velocity approaches zero, causing the period T to diverge logarithmically to infinity: T -> infinity!">
B. The period diverges logarithmically toward infinity ($T \to \infty$).
</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="false" data-explanation="Period increases monotonically with amplitude; it never drops to zero!">
C. The period approaches zero because potential energy is maximized.
</div>
</div>

<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-code">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">04 · Computational Implementation</div>
<h2>5.4 Exact Elliptic Period & Phase Orbit Integration</h2>
<p>Compute exact periods using complete elliptic integrals and integrate nonlinear trajectories with SciPy.</p>
</div>

<div class="code-box">
<div class="code-header">
<div class="code-tabs">
<button class="code-tab-btn active">Python (SciPy ellipk / solve_ivp)</button>
</div>
<button class="btn-copy">Copy Code</button>
</div>
<pre class="code-block"><code>import numpy as np
from scipy.special import ellipk
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

g, L = 9.81, 1.0
w0 = np.sqrt(g / L)
T0 = 2 * np.pi / w0

# Exact Period vs Linear Period for theta0 = 90 deg
theta0 = np.radians(90.0)
k = np.sin(theta0 / 2)
T_exact = (4.0 / w0) * ellipk(k**2)

print(f"Linear Period T0: {T0:.4f} s")
print(f"Exact Nonlinear Period T(90 deg): {T_exact:.4f} s (Ratio: {T_exact/T0:.3f})")

# Numerical Phase Plane Integration
def pendulum_ode(t, y):
    theta, omega = y
    return [omega, -w0**2 * np.sin(theta)]

sol = solve_ivp(pendulum_ode, [0, 10], [theta0, 0.0], max_step=0.01)</code></pre>
